{{Short description|Theorem in order theory}}
{{distinguish|Erdős–Dushnik–Miller theorem}}
In mathematics, the '''Dushnik–Miller theorem''' is a result in [[order theory]] stating that every [[Countable set|countably infinite]] [[linear order]] has a non-identity [[order embedding]] into itself.{{r|djm}} It is named for Ben Dushnik and E. W. Miller, who proved this result in a paper of 1940; in the same paper, they showed that the statement does not always hold for [[uncountable set|uncountable]] linear orders, using the [[axiom of choice]] to build a suborder of the [[real numbers|real line]] of [[Cardinal number|cardinality]] [[Continuum (set theory)|continuum]] with no non-identity order embeddings into itself.{{r|dm}}

In [[reverse mathematics]], the Dushnik–Miller theorem for countable linear orders has the same strength as the [[arithmetical comprehension axiom]] (ACA<sub>0</sub>), one of the "big five" subsystems of [[second-order arithmetic]].{{r|djm|hirschfeldt}} This result is closely related to the fact that (as [[Louise Hay (mathematician)|Louise Hay]] and Joseph Rosenstein proved) there exist [[computable set|computable]] linear orders with no computable non-identity self-embedding.{{r|hirschfeldt|rosenstein}}
